question: In the root grpc package's dial-option source file there is an unexported constructor that builds a functional option wrapping a single assignment: it stores the string it is handed as the fallback URI scheme on the internal option struct that the channel constructor later consults. Its doc comment explains that it exists so the legacy dialing entry point can keep falling back to "passthrough" name resolution while the newer client constructor falls back to "dns"; it sits between the test-only option that overrides the minimum connect deadline and the exported option that registers local resolver builders. Count only calls made from outside the file that defines it, and name each caller once even if a file defines several methods with that name. Name every function or method in the corpus that calls it, each as path::name.

evidence.contains: cc, err = NewClient(target, WithContextDialer(customDialer), withDefaultScheme("passthrough"), WithResolvers(res), WithTransportCredentials(insecure.NewCredentials()))

author_notes: The description pins the only unexported dial option in dialoptions.go whose closure assigns the fallback scheme field, distinguishing it from its neighbours that set the minimum connect deadline or the resolver list. Because the symbol is package-private it can only be used from the root grpc package: the legacy dialing entry point injects it ahead of user options, and two in-package tests pass it explicitly to pin the scheme they expect. Nothing else in the corpus references the symbol, so the caller set is exactly those three definitions.

question: The root credentials package has an experimental two-line reader that extracts a value from a context via the internal credentials package's own context accessor, type-asserts it to the exported struct that carries per-address attributes supplied by the resolver or balancer down to a transport credential's dialing-time negotiation, and returns that struct's zero value when nothing of that type is present. It sits directly after the declaration of that attribute-carrying struct and before the helper that compares a connection's security level. Count only calls made from outside the file that defines it, and name each caller once even if a file defines several methods with that name. Name every function or method in the corpus that calls it, each as path::name. Test functions count as callers; name them too.
author_notes: Two context readers live in that file; the described one is distinguished by asserting to the attribute-carrying struct rather than to the per-RPC request info and by returning a bare value with no ok flag. Its consumers are the two credential implementations that need resolver-supplied attributes at negotiation time — the xDS-aware cluster lookup used by the Google default credentials and the xDS credentials' own client-side negotiation — plus two definitions in the transport tests, a fake credential implementation and the test whose custom dialer reads the same attributes.

One of them takes a raw sequence-counter byte slice and reports which end of the connection owns it: if the high bit of the counter's final byte is set it returns the server end, otherwise the client end. It is the inverse of the two constructors in the same file that set that same high bit when initialising outgoing and incoming counters. Count only calls made from outside the file that defines it, and name each caller once even if a file defines several methods with that name. Name every function or method in the corpus that calls it, each as path::name. Test functions count as callers; name them too.

question: The metadata package's map-based header type has a method that adds extra values for a key without discarding what is already stored there: it returns immediately when no values are supplied, lowercases the key, and extends the existing slice held at that key with the new values. It sits between the method that replaces a key's whole value slice and the one that drops a key entirely, and its doc comment stresses that the key is lowercased before storing. Count only calls made from outside the file that defines it, and name each caller once even if a file defines several methods with that name. Name every function or method in the corpus that calls it, each as path::name. Test functions count as callers; name them too.
author_notes: The neighbouring methods either overwrite or delete, so "extend the existing values, lowercasing the key" identifies exactly one method on that type. Its callers are the RLS picker path that attaches the cached route-lookup header data onto an already-populated pick result, the metadata unit test that exercises the add-without-overwrite table, and the CSM plugin-option test that deliberately puts a second value under the metadata-exchange key. Other places that build headers use the pair constructors or the replacing setter instead.

question: The resolver package exposes a one-line accessor that returns the package-level variable holding the scheme applied when a dial target has no registered scheme of its own. It is the read counterpart of the initialisation-time setter just above it, which overwrites that variable and also records in an internal package that the user changed it; the doc comment notes the value seen by the legacy dialing entry point versus the "dns" fallback used by the newer client constructor. Count only calls made from outside the file that defines it, and name each caller once even if a file defines several methods with that name. Name every function or method in the corpus that calls it, each as path::name. Test functions count as callers; name them too.
author_notes: Only one function in the resolver package reads and returns that package-level fallback scheme variable; the setter next to it writes it, and the builder lookup takes a scheme argument instead. It is called from the RLS config parser when a lookup-service target lacks a scheme, from the channel helper that canonicalises a target after the user overrode the global default, and from the parsed-target test that computes the expected scheme for its table. Those three definitions are the complete set of references in the corpus.

question: In internal/transport/http_util.go there is a tiny unexported predicate over a single HTTP/2 header name whose entire body is a two-arm switch: it answers true only for ":authority" and "user-agent", the two protocol-owned names that must still be surfaced to users as metadata, and false for everything else. It is always consulted together with the sibling predicate that classifies a name as protocol-owned, to carve out that exception. Count only calls made from outside the file that defines it, and name each caller once even if a file defines several methods with that name. Name every function or method in the corpus that calls it, each as path::name. Test functions count as callers; name them too.
author_notes: Only one function in the corpus is a two-case switch returning true for exactly ":authority" and "user-agent"; its sibling reserved-name predicate lists many more names and returns true for any colon-prefixed name, so the description cannot match that one. The three callers are the only places that merge inbound HTTP/2 header fields into user-visible metadata: the net/http-backed server transport constructor and the header-handling routine of each of the two HTTP/2 transports; all three guard the same way and no other code needs the exception list.

It parses the digits with strconv.ParseUint, multiplies by the unit's duration, and clamps hour-scale values that would overflow math.MaxInt64 to the largest representable duration. Count only calls made from outside the file that defines it, and name each caller once even if a file defines several methods with that name. Name every function or method in the corpus that calls it, each as path::name. Test functions count as callers; name them too.

question: A short exported function in encoding/encoding.go stores a compression codec in the package-level map keyed by the codec's own reported name, and additionally appends that name to the shared slice of advertised compression names kept in internal/grpcutil when it is not already listed there. Its doc comment says it is not thread-safe, that it must only run during program start-up, and that the last registration for a given name wins. Count only calls made from outside the file that defines it, and name each caller once even if a file defines several methods with that name. Name every function or method in the corpus that calls it, each as path::name. Test functions count as callers; name them too.
author_notes: Two functions touch the compressor map, but only this one writes to it and also maintains the advertised-names slice; the lookup next to it merely indexes the map. The callers are the gzip package's package-level setup hook, the test that registers the same name twice, and the accepted-compression test in the root package that installs a stub codec. Other tests reach the registry through the internal testing-only indirection rather than calling this function, and call sites inside the defining file are not part of the set.

question: A one-line exported constructor in stats/opentelemetry/internal/tracing/carrier.go wraps a context.Context in the text-map adapter meant for the send side of an RPC and returns a pointer to it. The type it builds is the one whose Set appends a key/value pair to the context's outbound metadata, whose Keys enumerates that same outbound metadata, and whose Get does nothing but log an error because it is not usable in that direction. Production code needs it in a single place -- the client tracing handler that starts an attempt span and injects it into metadata -- and the rest of the set is its own unit test plus the two injection tests of the grpc-trace-bin propagator.

question: A four-line exported function in credentials/tls.go builds server-side transport credentials from two filesystem paths: it loads an X.509 certificate and its private key with tls.LoadX509KeyPair, returns that error unchanged on failure, and otherwise puts the loaded certificate as the sole entry of a tls.Config certificate list and hands that config to the package's generic constructor for TLS credentials. Its callers are all test helpers that need a real server certificate -- the credentials package's own gRPC server handshake helper, the xds server-credentials fallback helper, and the RLS test that gives the parent channel real transport credentials.

question: In credentials/alts/internal/conn/utils.go, an exported helper builds an ALTS 96-bit little-endian sequence counter struct out of bytes handed in by the caller: it records the given overflow length on the named result, copies the supplied slice into the struct's fixed-size array, and returns that named result with a bare return. question: In the root package of this corpus, an exported method on the type that hosts registered gRPC handlers takes a net.Listener, blocks, and returns an error. It marks the receiver as having started accepting; if the receiver was already shut down it closes the listener and returns the package's already-stopped sentinel error. Otherwise it registers a listen socket with channelz and loops on Accept, sleeping with a delay that doubles from 5ms up to one second on temporary accept failures and handing each accepted raw connection to its own goroutine. Count only calls made from outside the file that defines it, and name each caller once even if a file defines several methods with that name. Name every function or method in the corpus that calls it, each as path::name. Test functions count as callers; name them too.
author_notes: Only one method on that type takes a net.Listener and owns the accept loop with the doubling temporary-error backoff, which separates it from the HTTP handler entry point and from the shutdown methods it mentions. The corpus is the library itself rather than an application, so nothing in production code drives the accept loop; the callers are the two test fixtures that stand up a fake backend or handshaker and the two root-package tests that check shutdown behaviour.

question: The endpoint-sharding balancer package exports a one-argument accessor that takes a balancer picker and type-asserts it to the package's own aggregating picker, the one that delegates picks round-robin across its children and carries a slice of per-child status records alongside those delegates. The accessor is only useful where a petiole policy intercepts the aggregated state pushed up by endpoint sharding, which is why every caller is the state-forwarding hook of such a policy: least-request, ring hash and weighted round robin in production, plus the fake petiole in the package's own external test.

question: An exported method on the root package's server type takes a service descriptor and an implementation value and adds the pair to the server's table of served services. author_notes: The reflection-based handler-type check followed by delegation to the locking, duplicate-rejecting internal routine identifies the exported entry point rather than the unexported worker it wraps or the same-named interface method declared just above it. The remaining caller is the server test that registers a synthetic descriptor before inspecting the reported service information.

question: The pick-first balancer package exports an experimental one-argument function that takes a resolver state by value, stores a true boolean under an attribute key whose type is an unexported empty struct, and returns the updated state. The attribute is how a parent policy opts the leaf pick-first child into the generic health-reporting path used for client-side health checking and outlier detection. Name every function or method in the corpus that calls it, each as path::name. Test functions count as callers; name them too.
author_notes: Only one exported helper in the pick-first package rewrites a resolver state by attaching the private empty-struct-keyed opt-in attribute, so the behavioural description resolves to it alone. The opt-in has to be applied where a parent policy forwards resolver state down to its pick-first children, which is exactly why all four production callers are the resolver-state hooks of the petiole policies (least request, ring hash, round robin and weighted round robin). The other two callers are stub balancers inside pick-first's external test file that set the attribute before delegating to a real pick-first child.
